result: The authors detected 203 whole-chromosome-level alterations (86 amplifications, 117 deletions) across 32 cancer types. On average, 41-48% of genes on aneuploid chromosomes and 15-18% of genes on other chromosomes showed expression changes. At the proteome level, 24-33% of genes on aneuploid chromosomes showed changes.
evaluation: Claims C10-C12 and C41 provide consistent quantitative data from TCGA analysis with appropriate statistical methods (Wilcoxon test, differential expression analysis). The findings are supported by Figure 1C showing the percentages of differentially expressed genes/proteins across chromosomes. The methodology is clearly described and the results are internally consistent.

result: The authors identified 305 co-amplifications occurring more frequently than expected by chance, but found no significant difference in transcriptional dysregulation contribution between co-amplified and non-co-amplified chromosomes.
evaluation: Claims C13-C14 use appropriate statistical tests (chi-square test with multiple testing correction, paired Wilcoxon test) to assess co-amplification patterns. The finding that co-amplifications do not substantially contribute to overall transcriptional dysregulation on other chromosomes is supported by p=0.4 from paired Wilcoxon test and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C.

result: The authors observed stronger buffering at the proteome level compared to transcriptome level. For aneuploid chromosomes, 76.5-89.9% of proteomic changes showed corresponding transcriptomic changes, while for other chromosomes only 26.2-36.2% showed concordance, suggesting different regulatory mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C15, C45-C47 demonstrate differential regulation between aneuploid and non-aneuploid chromosomes through comparison of transcriptomic and proteomic data. The quantitative differences in concordance rates are substantial and support the conclusion that transcriptional control dominates for aneuploid chromosomes while post-transcriptional/post-translational control is more important for other chromosomes. Data shown in Figure 1C.

result: GO terms related to cell cycle and cell cycle processes are among the top dysregulated gene sets in aneuploid tumors.
evaluation: Claim C16 is supported by GO enrichment analysis of dysregulated genes (Supplementary file 2). This finding is biologically plausible given the known relationship between aneuploidy and cell proliferation, though the specific enrichment statistics are not provided in the main text.

result: Differentially abundant proteins on other chromosomes tend to be complex partners of differentially abundant proteins from aneuploid chromosomes. On average 4.47% (12.61% when considering only complex proteins) are partners, and these show significantly stronger abundance correlations than non-complex members.
evaluation: Claims C17-C20 use appropriate statistical tests (chi-square test, Wilcoxon test p<2.2e-16) with CORUM complex data. The finding of stronger correlations between co-complex members is shown in Figure 2A-B. The authors appropriately acknowledge the limited coverage of CORUM (22% of proteins) and adjust their interpretation accordingly.

result: Enrichment of protein-protein interactions between differentially abundant proteins on aneuploid and other chromosomes was found in 9/13 amplifications and 8/20 deletions. On average, 27.5% of differentially abundant proteins on other chromosomes interact with those on aneuploid chromosomes.
evaluation: Claims C21-C22 use appropriate randomization tests with HIPPIE PPI data (p<0.05) and are shown in Figure 2C. The higher percentage (27.5%) compared to complex-only analysis (4.47%) reflects the broader coverage of PPI data. The methodology is sound and results are consistent with the complex-based analysis.

result: Complex subunits are significantly depleted in differentially abundant proteins on other chromosomes for amplification cases but enriched for deletion cases.
evaluation: Claims C23-C24 use chi-square tests (p<0.05) with CORUM data and are shown in Figure 2D. The opposite patterns for amplifications versus deletions are biologically interpretable: amplifications may trigger selective maintenance of complex stoichiometry, while deletions may require upregulation of entire complexes. The statistical support is adequate.

result: Epigenetic regulation through DNA methylation does not substantially contribute to genome-wide gene expression changes induced by aneuploidy, with significant associations found in only ~7% of amplification and ~4% of deletion cases for downregulated genes.
evaluation: Claims C25-C27 use DNA methylation analysis with Wilcoxon tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B. The low percentage of cases showing significant methylation associations (6/86 amplifications, 5/117 deletions for downregulation) supports the conclusion. The control analysis comparing tumor vs normal samples strengthens the interpretation.

result: Transcription factor regulation does not explain the large transcriptional changes on other chromosomes, as randomization tests revealed no excess of TF targets among differentially expressed genes.
evaluation: Claim C28 uses appropriate randomization tests with ENCODE TF-target data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C. The control analysis with tumor vs normal samples and MYC targets demonstrates that the methodology can detect TF regulatory effects when present, strengthening the negative finding for aneuploidy-induced changes.

result: Top correlated co-complex members of aneuploid proteins have significantly higher numbers of ubiquitination sites, suggesting post-translational regulation (ubiquitin-mediated degradation) as a primary mechanism for maintaining protein complex stoichiometry.
evaluation: Claims C29-C30 use Wilcoxon test (p<0.05) with PhosphoSitePlus ubiquitination data shown in Figure 3B. The finding that top correlated partners have more ubiquitination sites is consistent with the hypothesis of post-translational control. However, C30 is an inference that could benefit from additional functional validation.

result: Aggregation-prone proteins on amplified chromosomes show stronger correlations with their complex partners compared to non-aggregating proteins (p<2.2e-16), suggesting upregulation of partners serves as a compensatory mechanism to prevent proteotoxicity. This pattern is not observed for aggregation-prone proteins on deleted chromosomes, but deleted proteins show stronger correlations with their aggregating co-complex members.
evaluation: Claims C31-C34 use Wilcoxon tests with aggregation data from Määttä et al., 2020, shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The asymmetric patterns for amplifications versus deletions are biologically interpretable and statistically significant. The logic that aggregation-prone proteins on amplified chromosomes need partner upregulation while those on deleted chromosomes do not is sound.

result: Promiscuous proteins (in >5 complexes) on amplified chromosomes show weaker correlations with partners compared to non-promiscuous proteins (p=6e-16). Proteins co-occurring in many complexes show stronger correlations than those found together infrequently.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 use Wilcoxon tests shown in Figure 4B-C with highly significant p-values. The finding that promiscuous proteins show weaker correlations is consistent with the model that proteins in fewer complexes require tighter stoichiometric control. The co-occurrence frequency analysis provides additional support for the complex organization hypothesis.

result: Top correlated proteins form complexes involved in translation, RNA splicing, RNA processing, and protein complex assembly. Deletion cases show stronger enrichment scores than amplification cases. Translation enrichment is largely driven by ribosomal proteins (23% of translation-related genes).
evaluation: Claims C37-C38 and C60 are based on functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5A-B and Supplementary file 6. The authors appropriately acknowledge that translation enrichment is driven by ribosomal genes and tested robustness by removing ribosomal genes and large complexes. The stronger enrichment in deletions versus amplifications is quantified and shown.

result: Samples with low stoichiometry deviation scores show a tendency toward lower survival probabilities across all three tissue types, though not significant in every case.
evaluation: Claim C39 is based on survival analysis shown in Figure 6B using Kaplan-Meier method. The authors acknowledge the results are not significant in every case, which weakens the conclusion. The stoichiometry deviation score methodology is novel but the survival association requires stronger statistical support. The tendency is observed but the evidence is insufficient to definitively support the claim.

result: Ubiquitin-binding proteins and proteasome components show significantly higher correlations between their abundances and stoichiometry deviation scores in two out of three tissues, suggesting activation of protein degradation machinery in tumors with poor stoichiometric compensation.
evaluation: Claim C40 uses correlation analysis with Wilcoxon tests shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, D. The finding is significant in 2/3 tissues and the pattern holds when samples are divided into amplification and deletion groups. This provides reasonable support for the hypothesis that proteotoxic stress activates degradation machinery, though the lack of significance in all tissues introduces some uncertainty.

result: The authors propose that protein complex subunits on other chromosomes maintain abundance levels unless they form complexes with differentially abundant aneuploid proteins. This co-abundance regulation depends on aggregation propensity and promiscuity of aneuploid partners, is controlled by post-translational mechanisms, and serves to prevent aggregation of unpaired complex members.
evaluation: Claims C61-C64 represent the main conclusions synthesizing multiple lines of evidence from C17-C36. The evidence for co-abundance patterns (C17-C24), lack of transcriptional/epigenetic control (C25-C28), ubiquitination signals (C29-C30), and aggregation/promiscuity effects (C31-C36) collectively support this model. The integration of multiple independent analyses strengthens the overall conclusion.

result: Complexes of the cellular core machinery are under functional selection to maintain stoichiometric balance in aneuploid tumors, particularly those involved in translation, RNA processing, and protein complex assembly.
evaluation: Claim C65 is supported by functional enrichment analysis (C37-C38) showing specific functions are protected. The consistency of enriched functions across amplifications and deletions suggests functional selection rather than just compensatory mechanisms. The evidence is adequate though the distinction between compensation and selection could be more clearly delineated.

result: Compensatory and functional maintenance mechanisms are established through post-translational control, and the degree of success in dealing with aneuploidy-induced stoichiometric imbalance impacts activation of protein degradation programs and patient survival.
evaluation: Claims C66-C67 represent overarching conclusions. C66 is well-supported by ubiquitination analysis (C29-C30) and lack of transcriptional/epigenetic signals (C25-C28). However, C67 regarding patient survival is less well-supported given the acknowledged lack of significance in all survival analyses (C39). The correlation with proteasome/ubiquitin-binding proteins (C40) is significant in only 2/3 tissues. The overall model is compelling but the survival impact requires stronger evidence.

result: The authors provide background on aneuploidy prevalence in tumors (~90%), prior findings on buffering effects at proteome level, post-transcriptional compensatory mechanisms in yeast and cancer, structural protein properties affecting buffering, post-translational regulation, and effects on genes on other chromosomes.
evaluation: Claims C1-C9 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These represent established background knowledge that contextualizes the current study. The citations appear accurate and relevant to the claims made.

result: The authors provide additional background and comparison to prior work, including similar findings in human cancer cells and yeast, consistent buffering patterns across systems, effects of aneuploidy on cell proliferation, stoichiometric imbalances, epigenetic mechanisms in cancer, ubiquitination as degradation signal, aggregation effects, and prior findings on compensatory mechanisms for CNAs.
evaluation: Claims C42-C44 and C49-C58 are supported by appropriate citations and represent accurate characterization of prior work. These claims provide important context for interpreting the current findings and comparing results across different experimental systems.

result: Up to 40% of differentially abundant proteins physically interact either in complexes or binary manner with partners on aneuploid chromosomes.
evaluation: Claim C48 synthesizes findings from C18-C22 regarding the percentage of differentially abundant proteins that are complex partners or PPI partners. The 40% figure represents the upper range and is supported by the PPI analysis showing 27.5% average interaction rate, with some cases exceeding 40%. The acknowledgment of incomplete interactome knowledge is appropriate.

result: 22% of proteins form part of at least one complex in CORUM database.
evaluation: Claim C59 is a factual statement about CORUM database coverage that is used to contextualize the complex-based analyses. This is an important caveat for interpreting the percentage of complex partners among differentially abundant proteins.
